segments.t: Camille returns to her office to find Sofia lounging comfortably after her photoshoot. What begins as casual office gossip quickly turns into a heated argument when Camille asks about Sofia's major film audition. Let's listen to their confrontation in French first.
Camille, Gabriel et Sarah se disputent!
Quoi? Ce n'est pas mon problème.
Tu as mis ça pour l'audition?
Non, je ne suis pas allée.
Pardon? Tu as manqué le rendez-vous?
Il y a une projection bientôt.
C'est beaucoup mieux comme ça.
J'ai travaillé dur pour ce rôle!
Attends, ce sont mes chaussures neuves?
Je les ai prises pour la photo.
Tu ne veux pas travailler, Sofia!
Tu ne veux pas être actrice.
Maintenant, reprends tes affaires et sors!
Voilà, je te rends tes chaussures!
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Camille, Gabriel et Sarah se disputent!
'Camille, Gabriel and Sarah are arguing!' Sofia eagerly shares the latest hallway drama. The reciprocal verb 'each other' means to argue or quarrel.
Quoi? Ce n'est pas mon problème.
'What? That is not my problem.' Camille brushes aside the gossip to focus on business. The negative 'ce n'est pas' means that is not.
Tu as mis ça pour l'audition?
'Did you wear that for the audition?' Camille points in disbelief at Sofia's extravagant golden dress. The past participle 'mis' comes from 'mettre', meaning to put on or wear.
Non, je ne suis pas allée.
'No, I did not go.' Sofia casually reveals that she skipped the meeting with the director. In the past tense with 'am', the participle 'gone' agrees with a feminine speaker.
Pardon? Tu as manqué le rendez-vous?
'Excuse me? You missed the appointment?' Camille can hardly believe what she is hearing. The verb 'missed' means to miss an event or appointment.
Il y a une projection bientôt.
'There is a screening soon.' Sofia claims she will meet the director casually at a movie screening instead. The feminine noun 'screening' refers to a film screening.
C'est beaucoup mieux comme ça.
'It is much better like that.' Sofia defends her spontaneous strategy. The adverb 'better' is the comparative form meaning better.
J'ai travaillé dur pour ce rôle!
'I worked hard for this role!' Camille reminds Sofia how much effort went into securing the casting call. Employed as an adverb, 'hard' means hard or intensely.
Attends, ce sont mes chaussures neuves?
'Wait, are those my new shoes?' Camille suddenly notices her own designer heels on Sofia's feet. The feminine plural adjective 'neuves' means brand-new.
Je les ai prises pour la photo.
'I took them for the photo.' Sofia confesses that she borrowed the shoes from Camille's office without asking. The participle 'prises' agrees in gender and number with the preceding pronoun 'les'.
Tu ne veux pas travailler, Sofia!
'You do not want to work, Sofia!' Camille loses her temper at her client's unprofessional attitude. The infinitive 'travailler' follows the negated verb 'vouloir'.
Tu ne veux pas être actrice.
'You do not want to be an actress.' Camille accuses Sofia of preferring celebrity glamour over real acting. In French, professions after 'to be' omit the indefinite article.
Maintenant, reprends tes affaires et sors!
'Now, take back your things and get out!' This everyday French sentence pairs 'now' with 'get out'.
Voilà, je te rends tes chaussures!

'There, I give you back your shoes!' Sofia angrily kicks off the heels and storms out of the room. The verb 'give back' means to return or give back. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.
Camille, Gabriel et Sarah se disputent!
Quoi? Ce n'est pas mon problème.
Tu as mis ça pour l'audition?
Non, je ne suis pas allée.
Pardon? Tu as manqué le rendez-vous?
Il y a une projection bientôt.
C'est beaucoup mieux comme ça.
J'ai travaillé dur pour ce rôle!
Attends, ce sont mes chaussures neuves?
Je les ai prises pour la photo.
Tu ne veux pas travailler, Sofia!
Tu ne veux pas être actrice.
Maintenant, reprends tes affaires et sors!
Voilà, je te rends tes chaussures!

Sofia marches out of the office barefoot, leaving Camille furious and exhausted. Looking down at her stretched-out designer shoes, Camille wonders how to salvage her client's career. Now let's listen to the scene one last time.
Tu as tout abîmé aujourd'hui!
